A fifth column is a group of people who are secretly working against the very group they appear to belong to — by helping that group's enemy from the inside.

Think of it this way: imagine you are in a castle that is under siege from an army outside. Your soldiers are defending the walls. But some people inside the castle — people who look like your friends and neighbors — are secretly unlocking back doors, poisoning the food supply, and passing information to the enemy outside. They smile at you during the day, but they are working against you at night. That is a fifth column.

The key ingredients are:

  • Disguise — they look like insiders, loyalists, or ordinary members of the group
  • Betrayal — they are actually loyal to an opposing side
  • Covert action — they work secretly, through sabotage, spying, spreading confusion, or giving the enemy an advantage
What Makes It Different From a Regular Spy or Traitor

A spy or a traitor is usually one person. A fifth column is a collective — a network, a group, sometimes a whole community of people who are coordinated in their hidden opposition. It implies an organized, deliberate effort from within, not just one bad apple.

Also, a spy sneaks into enemy territory from the outside. A fifth column is already there — embedded within the group, pretending to be one of them.
The Kinds of Actions a Fifth Column Takes

A fifth column doesn't usually fight openly. Instead, they operate in the shadows. Their work might include:

  • Spreading misinformation — planting false rumors or propaganda to weaken morale or cause confusion
  • Sabotage — quietly destroying supplies, infrastructure, or communication channels
  • Intelligence gathering — collecting sensitive information and leaking it to the enemy
  • Blocking decisions — influencing leadership from within to make bad choices that benefit the enemy
  • Creating division — stirring up internal conflict so the group tears itself apart

The goal is always to weaken the host group from the inside so the external enemy finds it easier to defeat or control them.

In its most literal and serious sense, fifth column is used in the context of war and national security — describing citizens of a country who secretly serve a foreign power or enemy nation. During wartime, governments have historically feared fifth columns because an enemy within is far more dangerous than one at the gates.

But the term has expanded well beyond war. Today, you will find it used in:

  • Politics — to accuse political opponents or certain groups of secretly serving foreign interests or working to undermine the state
  • Business — to describe employees or executives who are quietly sabotaging their own company for a competitor's benefit
  • Social movements — to describe people who infiltrate a movement and work to destroy it from within
  • Journalism and commentary — as a rhetorical label for anyone seen as an internal enemy
An Important Nuance: It Can Be Used Unfairly

Here is something critical to understand: the label "fifth column" is sometimes thrown at innocent people unfairly. Because the accusation involves hidden loyalty, it is very hard to disprove — you cannot easily prove that you are not secretly working for the enemy. This makes it a powerful and dangerous accusation.

Throughout history, governments and leaders have misused the term to target minority groups, immigrants, political dissidents, or anyone they found suspicious or inconvenient — even when those people were completely loyal. The mere suspicion of being a fifth column has been used to justify persecution, mass detention, and discrimination. So when you encounter this term, it is worth asking: is it being used based on real, documented evidence of betrayal, or is it being used loosely to attack a disfavored group?

A fifth column is a hidden group of people inside a country, organization, or community who secretly work to undermine it on behalf of an outside enemy — through deception, sabotage, espionage, or manipulation — while pretending to be loyal members.

The danger of a fifth column is precisely its invisibility. The threat does not come charging at you from outside — it is already sitting at your table.
